title: Bold as a leopard (Avot 5:20)
hook: Yehuda ben Tema: bold as a leopard, light as an eagle, swift as a deer, strong as a lion to do God's will
tomorrow: why read the same old text again and again?

segments.voice: Yesterday, David and Jonathan: love without conditions, parted and never ended. Today, a question about nerve.

Some people can ask anyone for anything: a better seat, a refund, a second chance. Others would rather go without than ask. Plenty of people sit in between, rehearsing the request and never sending it. So is it bold, or just rude, to ask for a favor? Avot has a sage who wants you fearless, and in the very next breath, the same sage warns against a face with no shame.
screen: `ASK FOR ANYTHING?` → `REHEARSED, NEVER SENT.` → `BOLD, OR JUST RUDE?`

segments.voice: Yehuda ben Tema says: be bold as a leopard, light as an eagle, swift as a deer and strong as a lion, to do the will of your Father in heaven. Then he says: the brazen-faced are bound for Gehinnom; the shamefaced, for the Garden of Eden. Bold, and yet not brazen. Readers argue over that seam. One side leans on the animals. The Shulchan Aruch, a code of Jewish law, opens with this saying, and its first paragraph explains the leopard: don't be embarrassed before people who mock you for doing right. On this view, shyness can keep good things from happening. Say the thing. Ask for the favor. Get up and do it. The other side leans on the next line. Shame isn't only a weakness here; it's what keeps boldness from turning into a face that can't blush. The Talmud names bashfulness as a mark of Abraham's children. On this view, the leopard is only for the will of heaven, and the bold need a brake. The mishnah keeps both, side by side. A leopard for the good thing. A face that can still blush while doing it.
screen: `LEOPARD, EAGLE, DEER, LION.` · `THE BRAZEN AND THE SHAMEFACED.` · `ONE SIDE: DON'T BE SHAMED OUT OF DOING RIGHT.` · `OTHER SIDE: SHAME IS THE BRAKE.` · then, large: `BOLD AS A LEOPARD.`

segments.voice: Stand, if you can, feet planted, shoulders back, the way you'd stand before saying something hard. Name one good thing you've been too shy to do or ask, and say it once, out loud, in a plain voice. Then soften your face, and keep standing for the rest of the sit.
screen: `STAND, FEET PLANTED.` · `NAME THE GOOD THING.` · `A SOFT FACE.`

segments.voice: Bold as a leopard: Yehuda ben Tema's first animal. Bold for doing right, and never brazen-faced.
The leopard, with a blush: bold as a leopard, for the good thing. Fifty-three days into Avot.

Yehuda ben Tema.meaning: a sage of the Mishnah, quoted in Avot 5:20

Gehinnom.meaning: in rabbinic teaching, a place of punishment and cleansing

Shulchan Aruch.meaning: a code of Jewish law; the name means set table

Talmud.meaning: the rabbis' long discussion built on the Mishnah

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 79a (bashfulness as a mark of Abraham's descendants)

notes: Avot 5:20 paraphrased: Yehuda ben Tema: be bold as a leopard, light as an eagle, swift as a deer and strong as a lion to do the will of your Father in heaven. He used to say: the brazen-faced to Gehinnom, the shamefaced to the Garden of Eden. Confirm.
Shulchan Aruch OC 1:1 opens with this saying (in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch) and explains bold as a leopard as not being embarrassed before mockers. Confirm wording.
Yevamot 79a: the descendants of Abraham are marked by being merciful, bashful and doing kindness. Script says 'names bashfulness as a mark of Abraham's children'. Confirm.
Debate: the two sides (don't be shamed out of doing right / shame as the brake) are both drawn from the text and its readers, not attributed to named schools.
